extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journalists, policy analysts, and general readers interested in media freedom and censorship in Bhutan
extracted.subtask_description: Encyclopedic summary of laws, institutions, incidents, and practices that shape censorship and media freedom in Bhutan, including statutory powers, enforcement patterns, and examples of restrictions on press and Internet expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of laws guaranteeing right to information
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no laws that either guarantee citizens' right to information or explicitly structure a censorship scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that Bhutan does not yet have any legislation guaranteeing the citizens' right to information, which affects journalists' and citizens' access to official information and contributes to difficulty obtaining information from bureaucrats and public officials (especially on corruption).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on ownership of media and licensing of journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Censorship is conducted by restrictions on the ownership of media outlets and licensing of journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bhutan has one government majority-owned newspaper (Kuensel), five private newspapers, several magazines, and three ISPs; the regulatory environment and licensing/ownership rules shape who can operate media and the diversity of viewpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government majority ownership and editorial influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of a government majority-owned newspaper (Kuensel) and state influence on editorial coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The state-owned newspaper and other media outlets often publish articles favorable to the government and cover criticism only occasionally, indicating structural influence through ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controls on advertising as a lever of media regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Government may propose controls on advertising (example: May 2007 proposal) to influence media operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2007 government proposal to control advertising was withdrawn after unfavorable newspaper editorials, showing how regulatory proposals can affect media economics and editorial stance even if not enacted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restricting press access to official events
rubrics_metrics.description: Officials may permit only government media or 'authorized' private media to attend certain functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: during the Indian PM's visit in May 2008, only journalists from Bhutan Broadcasting Service and Kuensel were permitted; officials may respond only to government or authorized media, restricting independent coverage of state events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occasional government blocking of Internet content deemed pornographic or offensive
rubrics_metrics.description: Government occasionally blocks access to Web sites containing pornography or information deemed offensive to the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freedom House reported that blocked information typically does not extend to political content, but blocking for pornography/offensive material occurs; enforcement patterns may be selective.

rubrics_metrics.name: High levels of self-censorship among media practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite few reports of official intimidation, there are high levels of self-censorship among Bhutanese media practitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freedom House and other reports describe widespread self-censorship, which limits critical reporting even when direct censorship is infrequent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation and selective blocking of online forums
rubrics_metrics.description: Official forums may be moderated and some news portals have faced temporary blocks (e.g., bhutantimes.com in 2007).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuensel's official forums allow open criticism but are moderated; bhutantimes.com was temporarily blocked by BICMA reportedly because discussions were criticism of a minister, illustrating forum-level moderation and selective blocking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory censorship reflecting individual sensitivities
rubrics_metrics.description: BICMA's censorship pattern appears to reflect individual sensitivities of people who may have been discussed online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article suggests blocking decisions sometimes respond to complaints about particular individuals rather than consistent public-interest standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal liability for journalists' social media posts and restrictions on civil servants' speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists can face criminal charges for posts on personal Facebook accounts; law states 'A civil servant shall not critique his agency and the Royal Government.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From 2016–2018, prosecutions of journalists for Facebook posts (even about true facts) resulted in prison sentences and heavy fines, showing social-media speech criminalization and specific restrictions on civil servants' critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bhutan Information Communications & Media Act (2006): broad regulatory discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act provides for considerable discretion, including consideration of 'peace, stability and well-being' in taking over communications services and facilities and broad regulatory powers for BICMA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Act established BICMA and grants it wide-ranging authority that can be invoked in the national interest; its language (e.g., 'peace, stability and well-being') supplies broad justifications for regulatory action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to intercept communications
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act authorizes intercepting communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bhutan's media law includes explicit provisions enabling interception of communications, which can affect privacy and surveillance of journalists and citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory rulemaking and issuance of permits to publish
rubrics_metrics.description: BICMA is empowered to perform regulatory rulemaking and issue permits to publish materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitting regimes shape who may publish and under what conditions; failure to obtain or comply can trigger penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to regulate audiovisual content (films, dramas, shows)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act authorizes regulation of showing films, performing dramas, and related media activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific sections cited (e.g., show films, perform dramas) indicate content and performance regulation powers that can limit creative and journalistic expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to block protest websites and ban certain foreign publications
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act enables blocking access to protest websites and banning certain foreign publications in the national interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These powers provide a statutory basis for suppressing protest-related online content and restricting foreign media seen as contrary to national interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalties and search/seizure powers for regulatory violations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act provides penalties for failure to comply with prohibitory orders and empowers the government to enter private property to search and seize when the agency 'reasonably suspects' regulatory violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement mechanisms include fines, other penalties, and intrusion into private premises based on regulatory suspicion, which can chill reporting and expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: National Security Act (1992): prohibition on criticism of the king and political system
rubrics_metrics.description: Several provisions prohibit criticism of the king and the political system; the Act punishes those who undermine or attempt to undermine Bhutan's security by creating or inciting 'hatred and disaffection,' including by speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute is broad and criminalizes a range of speech acts framed as threats to security or public order, constraining political expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal penalties under National Security Act for undermining security (up to 10 years)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imprisonment for up to ten years for those who undermine or attempt to undermine Bhutan's security by creating or inciting 'hatred and disaffection.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Severe maximum penalties create strong deterrence against speech judged to harm national security or public order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalties for creating misunderstanding/hostility between government and foreign peoples (up to 5 years)
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech that creates 'misunderstanding or hostility between the government and people of Bhutan and the Government and people of any foreign country' is punishable by up to five years' imprisonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision criminalizes speech that could impact foreign relations, extending censorship reach to statements about foreign-policy-sensitive topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalties for promoting enmity between groups and disturbing public tranquility (up to 3 years)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act allows up to three years' imprisonment for those who speak or act to promote 'feelings of enmity or hatred between different religious, racial or language groups or castes and communities' or commit acts prejudicial to maintenance of harmony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While framed as hate-speech and public-order protection, such provisions can constrain robust debate on sensitive societal divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminalization of hate speech and propaganda harmful to foreign relations
rubrics_metrics.description: The National Security Act criminalizes hate speech and propaganda harmful to foreign relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These bans are explicitly named in the Act, providing statutory grounds for prosecution of certain categories of expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tobacco Control Act (2010): content-based restriction on depictions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tobacco Control Act of 2010 makes depictions of tobacco use in motion media other than for health promotion constitute a petty misdemeanor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an example of content-based media restriction tied to public-health regulation that can limit portrayals in films and broadcasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media law may expand outlets without protecting journalists or guaranteeing FOI
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2006 media law led to establishment of independent radio stations but did not provide specific protections for journalists or guarantee freedom of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal reforms can increase media plurality in form while failing to secure press freedom in substance, leaving journalists vulnerable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional provision for freedom of speech with qualified respect in practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitution provides for freedom of speech including for members of the press, and the government generally respects these rights in practice, but other laws and practices impose limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although constitutional protections exist (and prohibit arbitrary/unlawful interference with privacy and reputation), statutory provisions and enforcement practices (and self-censorship) mean practical limits persist.
